verdict.rationale: Convergent verbs of real becoming and shared substance predicate full human nature of Jesus across several NT corpora. John 1.14 uses ginomai in the aorist (ho logos sarx egeneto), a verb of entering a state of being, not a verb of seeming. Hebrews 2.14 stacks koinoneo (perfect) and metecho (aorist) of haima kai sarx, Heb 2.16 sets angelic nature against sperma Abraam, Heb 2.17 and Heb 4.15 twice say kata panta likeness to the brothers, and 1 John 4.2 makes Iesoun Christon en sarki eleluthota (perfect participle) a confessional test. Direct concordance confirms the same ginomai plus sarx plus sperma cluster in Rom 1.3, Phil 2.7, and Gal 4.4, so the pattern is broad, not isolated. Confidence is high because the witness is dense, multi-author, and the only readings that resist it are foreclosed by the becoming verbs and the predicated death. pan_canonical is false because the predicating lemmas are NT-only, though OT seed and resurrection texts are cross-referenced.

scripture.force: The clause καὶ ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο puts the aorist ἐγένετο (lemma γίνομαι, confirmed in the store) with the predicate σάρξ. ginomai is a verb of coming to be in a state, not of appearing to be, so the Word came to exist as human flesh. ἐσκήνωσεν ἐν ἡμῖν then locates that flesh dwelling among the community who saw glory, which fixes the becoming as concrete, not notional.

Two near-synonymous sharing verbs intensify the claim. The παιδία κεκοινώνηκεν (perfect of κοινωνέω) of αἷμα καὶ σάρξ, and αὐτὸς παραπλησίως μετέσχεν (aorist of μετέχω) τῶν αὐτῶν. παραπλησίως means in closely like manner, and the shared referent is human flesh and blood. The purpose clause ἵνα διὰ τοῦ θανάτου presupposes a mortal nature he can die in.

ἀπαλλάξῃ τούτους, ὅσοι φόβῳ θανάτου διὰ παντὸς τοῦ ζῆν ἔνοχοι ἦσαν δουλείας. The Son shares flesh and blood so that through his own death he frees those bound by fear of death. Death-capacity is predicated of him, and capacity to die is a feature of human nature, not of the divine nature, so the verse reinforces real humanity.

οὐ γὰρ δήπου ἀγγέλων ἐπιλαμβάνεται ἀλλὰ σπέρματος Ἀβραὰμ ἐπιλαμβάνεται. The οὐ ... ἀλλά construction explicitly denies angelic nature and affirms the seed of Abraham, that is human descent, as what is taken hold of. Even on the softer help sense of ἐπιλαμβάνομαι the recipients are still human seed, so the human reference is fixed either way.

ὤφειλεν κατὰ πάντα τοῖς ἀδελφοῖς ὁμοιωθῆναι. ὁμοιωθῆναι (lemma ὁμοιόω, confirmed in the store) is an aorist passive infinitive, made like, and κατὰ πάντα is a universal quantifier, in every respect. The obligation is tied to his function as a merciful and faithful high priest. The all leaves no constituent of human nature reserved.

πεπειρασμένον κατὰ πάντα καθ’ ὁμοιότητα χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας. πεπειρασμένον (lemma πειράζω) is a perfect passive participle, a settled state of having been tested. He was tested in every way according to the likeness of our condition, with sin alone excluded. Genuine testing and συμπαθέω (sympathy) presuppose a human will and affective life that can actually be tested.

πᾶν πνεῦμα ὃ ὁμολογεῖ Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ἐν σαρκὶ ἐληλυθότα ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ ἐστιν. ἐληλυθότα (lemma ἔρχομαι, confirmed in the store) is a perfect active participle, so the having come in flesh is a fixed, abiding state. ἐν σαρκὶ marks the embodied human nature as the very mode of the coming, which is the apostolic test of true confession.

πᾶν πνεῦμα ὃ μὴ ὁμολογεῖ τὸν Ἰησοῦν ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ οὐκ ἔστιν, καὶ τοῦτό ἐστιν τὸ τοῦ ἀντιχρίστου. The refusal to confess Jesus come in flesh is branded the spirit of antichrist. This obverse polemic presupposes that in-flesh coming is a non-negotiable confession, which confirms the positive predication of 4.2.

τοῦ γενομένου ἐκ σπέρματος Δαυὶδ κατὰ σάρκα. Direct concordance shows the same lemma cluster as the anchors, γίνομαι plus σπέρμα plus σάρξ, here predicated of the Son. He came to be from the seed of David according to flesh, which is a literal human-descent statement and widens the pattern into the Pauline corpus.

ἐν ὁμοιώματι ἀνθρώπων γενόμενος (lemma γίνομαι, confirmed in the store) καὶ σχήματι εὑρεθεὶς ὡς ἄνθρωπος. The participle of γίνομαι again says he came to be, and ἀνθρώπων names the kind. ὁμοίωμα carries a likeness sense that, taken alone, a reader could press toward appearance only, so this verse is both a witness and the lexical seam where the contrary reading tries to enter.

ἐξαπέστειλεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ, γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός, γενόμενον ὑπὸ νόμον. The store confirms γενόμενον (lemma γίνομαι) twice. Born of a woman is a literal human-birth predicate, the same becoming verb used in John 1.14 and Rom 1.3, which extends the convergent pattern and roots it in ordinary human generation.

ἐν ὁμοιώματι σαρκὸς ἁμαρτίας. The store confirms ὁμοίωμα plus σάρξ here. The phrase likeness of sinful flesh is the strongest lexical foothold for a reading that softens the humanity, because ὁμοίωμα can mean a copy or semblance. It is recorded as a complicating text, but the surrounding becoming and death verbs and the parallel plain statements in Rom 1.3 and Heb 2.14 prevent ὁμοίωμα from meaning mere appearance.

complicating_texts.resolution: ἐν ὁμοιώματι σαρκὸς ἁμαρτίας uses ὁμοίωμα, likeness or semblance, which in isolation could be pressed toward an appearance-only humanity. The store shows ὁμοίωμα is rare, 6 occurrences, so its sense is set by context. Here the qualifier is ἁμαρτίας, not σαρκός. The likeness is to SINFUL flesh, marking the absence of sin, not the absence of real flesh. The plain becoming statements Rom 1.3 and Gal 4.4 by the same author, and Heb 2.14 sharing of flesh and blood, fix σάρξ as literal, so ὁμοίωμα cannot reduce to mere appearance.

ἐν ὁμοιώματι ἀνθρώπων and σχήματι ὡς ἄνθρωπος pair ὁμοίωμα with σχῆμα, form or fashion, a near-hapax with a single store occurrence. Read alone these could suggest semblance. But the controlling verb is γενόμενος, came to be, the same γίνομαι of John 1.14, and the likeness language describes the real human condition he entered, not a costume. The verse stands as a witness to humanity once γίνομαι anchors it.

χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας could be read as subtracting an integral part of the kata panta likeness. The text distinguishes being tested from sinning. Sin is a defect in the exercise of human nature, not a constituent of it, so its absence preserves a non-fallen instance of full humanity rather than an incomplete one.

ἐπιλαμβάνομαι, 19 occurrences, can mean take hold of a nature or help. On either sense the οὐ ... ἀλλά contrast still locates the object in σπέρματος Ἀβραάμ, human descent, and Heb 2.14 and 2.17 settle assumed human nature on independent lexical grounds, so the verdict does not hang on resolving this verb.

variant_units_examined.note: The λύει τὸν Ἰησοῦν reading attested in some witnesses and patristic citation, versus the μὴ ὁμολογεῖ reading present in the queried store text, does not change the verdict. Both readings target denial of Jesus come in flesh, so both presuppose the in-flesh confession as the apostolic norm.

variants.note: None of the anchor verses falls in the ingested ECM window of 3 John 1.1 to 1.15, so no published apparatus was examined. The 1 John 4.3 locus is treated from the queried store text and standard variant knowledge, and it is not verdict-flipping.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Takes γίνομαι in John 1.14, Rom 1.3, Phil 2.7, Gal 4.4 as a real change of state into the human condition, σάρξ and αἷμα as literal substance, and the predicated θάνατος as genuine mortality. On this reading the kata panta of Heb 2.17 and 4.15 closes off any reserved part of human nature, and 1 John 4.2 makes the confession a test.

competing_lens_verdicts.verdict: not sustainable on the lexical data
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: In its strongest form this lens leans on the likeness words, ὁμοίωμα in Rom 8.3 and Phil 2.7 and σχῆμα in Phil 2.7, to argue that Jesus only seemed human. The lens is represented fairly because those words do carry a semblance sense. But ginomai is a becoming verb not a seeming verb, the flesh and blood are said to be shared and partaken, and his death is predicated as the means of redemption, so the likeness words are qualified by real-becoming and real-dying language and cannot bear an appearance-only weight.

competing_lens_verdicts.verdict: not sustainable on the lexical data
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: In its strongest form this lens grants real flesh but reserves a higher human faculty, for example a rational soul, from the assumption. It is represented fairly because the bundle names σάρξ and αἷμα directly but does not carry a ψυχή or νοῦς anchor lemma. The reading still fails because κατὰ πάντα in Heb 2.17 and 4.15 is an unrestricted universal, made like the brothers in every respect, and genuine πειράζω testing and συμπαθέω sympathy require an interior human life, so no constituent is left reserved except sin.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict rests on convergent lexical evidence, γίνομαι plus σάρξ in John 1.14 and Rom 1.3, μετέχω and κοινωνέω plus σάρξ καὶ αἷμα in Heb 2.14, γίνομαι plus γυνή in Gal 4.4, ἐπιλαμβάνομαι plus σπέρμα Ἀβραάμ in Heb 2.16, ὁμοιόω plus κατὰ πάντα in Heb 2.17 and 4.15, and ὁμολογέω plus ἐν σαρκὶ ἐληλυθότα in 1 John 4.2. The likeness words ὁμοίωμα and σχῆμα are the only lexical seam a contrary reading can use, and the surrounding becoming and death verbs close it.

stem_audit.notes: The stem states a positive predication plus a constitutive list, body and rational soul. The body component is directly lexicalized by σάρξ, αἷμα, and θάνατος across the anchors and the Pauline parallels. The rational soul component is not carried by a dedicated ψυχή or νοῦς anchor lemma in the bundle, so it is established indirectly through the unrestricted κατὰ πάντα of Heb 2.17 and 4.15 and through πειράζω testing and συμπαθέω sympathy, which require human cognitive and affective faculties. The verdict therefore holds on the universal quantifier even though no specific interior-faculty lemma anchors it. The stem is not tradition-loaded, so neutralized_form is null.

lay_summary: The proposition is that Jesus has a complete human nature. The Greek vocabulary across John, Hebrews, Romans, Philippians, and Galatians points the same direction, and a direct search of the text confirms the words really cluster this way rather than appearing once. John 1.14 says the Word became flesh, using ginomai, a verb of coming to be in a state, not a verb of seeming. Hebrews 2.14 stacks two sharing verbs, koinoneo and metecho, both saying Jesus partook of the same flesh and blood as the children he came to rescue, and the next verses tie this to his real death. Hebrews 2.16 contrasts taking hold of angelic nature with taking hold of the seed of Abraham, that is human descent. Hebrews 2.17 and 4.15 twice use the phrase kata panta, in every respect, made like the brothers and tested under the likeness of human experience, with sin alone excluded. First John 4.2 makes confession of Jesus come in flesh a test of true prophecy, and 4.3 brands its denial as the spirit of antichrist. The same becoming verb recurs in Romans 1.3, born of David's seed according to flesh, and Galatians 4.4, born of a woman, so the pattern is broad. Where does room for disagreement come from. It comes from one family of words. Romans 8.3 and Philippians 2.7 say he came in the likeness of flesh and in the fashion of a man, and the word for likeness can by itself mean a mere semblance. A reader could press that toward seeming rather than being. But the search shows that word is rare, and in context it is paired with the becoming verb and qualified by the word sinful, so it marks the absence of sin, not the absence of real flesh. The body is named directly, and the interior human life is required by genuine temptation and priestly sympathy, so no part of human nature is held back except sin.
